paper.title: GAIA: A Benchmark for General AI Assistants

read_sources.note: Used for arXiv metadata, author list, abstract, benchmark size, public leaderboard framing, and human/GPT-4 headline scores.
Read for benchmark philosophy, question examples, levels, design goals, dataset split, tool-use/multimodal requirements, evaluation, and limitations.
Used to confirm benchmark hosting context.

summary.one_sentence: GAIA evaluates general AI assistants with concise, factoid real-world questions that are easy for humans but require AI systems to browse, reason, handle multimodal evidence, and use tools accurately.
summary.thesis: The benchmark rejects the idea that harder-for-humans exams are the best path to AGI evaluation; instead, it targets simple human tasks whose answer is easy to check but whose execution path is complex for current assistants.
summary.why_it_matters: For agents, GAIA is a clean benchmark of compound assistant behavior: the answer is usually short, but reaching it requires correct tool use, web navigation, evidence synthesis, and exact formatting.

prior_state: Many LLM benchmarks were becoming saturated or were vulnerable to data contamination.
Some benchmarks target tasks that are difficult for humans, even though current AI systems can already outperform non-experts on professional exams.
Open-ended generation evaluation can require expensive human or model-based judging.
General assistants need evaluation on real-world multi-step tasks with unambiguous answers.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks how to evaluate general assistant robustness on practical tasks whose solutions are easy to verify but hard for AI systems to execute reliably.
assumptions: Concise factual answers allow simple automatic grading.
Questions should be conceptually simple for non-expert humans.
Most questions should require real tool use, browsing, multimodality, or multi-step reasoning rather than memorized text.
Withholding some answers can support a leaderboard while reducing leakage.

concepts.name: General AI assistant
concepts.definition: An AI system expected to handle broad real-world user questions through reasoning, tools, browsing, and multimodal processing.

concepts.name: Factoid answer
concepts.definition: A concise, unambiguous answer that can be automatically checked.

concepts.name: Conceptually simple task
concepts.definition: A task that average humans can understand and solve robustly, even if it requires several steps.

concepts.name: Difficulty level
concepts.definition: A grouping of GAIA questions by required complexity, from easier Level 1 tasks to harder Level 3 tasks.

concepts.name: Held-out answers
concepts.definition: Answers withheld from public release to support leaderboard evaluation.

concepts.name: Reasoning trace
concepts.definition: The sequence of steps or evidence used to derive the final answer, useful for interpretability and contamination checks.

method.core_idea: Craft questions that require real-world tool use and multi-step evidence gathering, make final answers short and unique, collect human baselines, and publish a split with held-out answers for leaderboard evaluation.
action_grammar: question: real-world prompt with one concise factual answer.
evidence: optional image, document, web page, or clue used to answer.
tools: browser, search, code, calculator, multimodal parser, or other assistant capability.
answer string: final concise response checked against ground truth.
leaderboard split: questions with hidden answers.
steps: Design questions that are simple for humans but require tool-use, browsing, reasoning, or multimodal handling for AI.
Ensure answers are concise, factual, unique, and unlikely to appear directly in training data.
Group tasks into levels of increasing difficulty.
Evaluate GPT-4 with plugins and other assistants on the same questions.
Withhold answers to 300 questions for leaderboard evaluation.
Use exact/factual answer matching rather than free-form open-ended judging.
method.pseudocode:
for question in gaia:
    evidence = question.attachments_or_web_context
    agent_trace = agent.solve(question.prompt, tools=[browser, code, calculator, vision])
    answer = normalize(agent_trace.final_answer)
    success = exact_or_rule_match(answer, question.ground_truth)
    record(success, level=question.level)

claims.statement: GAIA contains 466 carefully crafted questions targeting general AI assistant abilities.
caveats: The benchmark is deliberately small and curated rather than a large scraped dataset.

claims.statement: GAIA questions require abilities such as reasoning, multimodal handling, web browsing, and tool-use proficiency.
caveats: Not every question requires every ability.

claims.statement: GAIA uses concise, unambiguous factual answers to support simple automatic evaluation.
caveats: Some normalization and answer-format rules still matter.

claims.statement: Human respondents score 92% on GAIA, while GPT-4 equipped with plugins scores 15% in the paper's headline comparison.
caveats: This is paper-era GPT-4-with-plugins performance and not current leaderboard SOTA.

claims.statement: GPT-4 with tools does not exceed 30% on the easiest tasks and scores 0% on the hardest tasks in the paper's discussion.
caveats: Exact setup and tool access affect assistant performance.

claims.statement: The authors release 166 annotated developer questions and hold out 300 answers for a leaderboard.
caveats: Leaderboard integrity depends on answer secrecy and contamination management.

evidence.result: The paper states GAIA comprises 466 carefully crafted questions and answers.
The paper says GAIA tasks require reasoning, multimodality, web browsing, and tool-use proficiency, with examples involving NIH pages, Wikipedia calculations, and NASA/APOD image evidence.
GAIA questions are designed to have unique, factual, concise, unambiguous answers so evaluation is simple and robust.
The paper reports 92% human performance versus 15% for GPT-4 equipped with plugins.
The paper says GPT-4 with tools does not exceed 30% on the easiest GAIA tasks and scores 0% on the hardest tasks.
The authors release 166 annotated developer questions and keep 300 answers hidden for a leaderboard.

agent_infra_takeaways: GAIA is a clean assistant benchmark because the final answer is short but the path is operationally complex.
Tool-use evaluation should ask whether the tool was needed and used correctly, not merely whether the model can name a tool.
Concise factoid answers make grading cheaper and less judge-dependent than free-form reports.
The human-vs-AI gap is useful because these are not expert-only tasks; they measure robustness on ordinary information work.
Agents need provenance capture for GAIA-like tasks: web pages, calculations, images, and intermediate facts should be auditable.
GAIA's held-out split is a reminder that benchmark operations matter: answer secrecy and contamination control are part of the benchmark.
caveats: The benchmark is small and curated.
Paper-era GPT-4/plugin results are historical, not current SOTA.
Exact answer matching can be brittle if normalization rules are underspecified.
Some tasks depend on web state that can drift unless evidence is fixed or reproduced.
GAIA evaluates final factoid answers more than full side-effecting task completion.
Leaderboard integrity depends on keeping held-out answers from leaking.
